The universal lens unifies these as a quadratic form on the drive vector, measuring how efficiently a quarterback converts possessions into expected points while accounting for his role in the offensive scheme. The GSE mapping uses a bilinear state-transition model to derive carry probability and pass rate from fundamental play conversion matrices, ensuring internal consistency across all 21 QBs. The GSI mapping models EPA per drive as a Gaussian process conditioned on TTT and pressure rate, enabling probabilistic salary calibration. Cross-layer veto conditions enforce that no QB can simultaneously have high carry probability and low TTT—this would indicate either a running back disguised as a QB or a severe injury affecting throwing mechanics. Historical genealogy traces back to Sabermetrics' Win Shares and ESPN's Total Quarterback Rating, evolving into modern state-space models used by companies like Second Spectrum. Theory of mind considerations highlight coaching staff decisions: coaches may bench a QB with high TTT if they believe improved mobility will reduce sacks, even if raw EPA remains unchanged. Failure modes include over-reliance on box-score statistics (e.g., QB Rating) and ignoring contextual factors like weather (e.g., Tampa Bay storms) or roster changes (e.g., Drake London out).
